40: Lectures three and four: data types and structures. Today we look at how data is measured, how it is organised, and how it behaves over time. We cover scales of measurement, discrete versus continuous data, structured versus semi structured data, text data, and time series.
41: Here are the five building blocks for this lecture. One, the four scales of measurement and what maths each one allows. Two, discrete versus continuous data, which means countable values versus measurements on a scale. Three, structured versus semi structured data, rows and columns versus flexible tagged data. Four, text data structure basics, meaning how unstructured text is broken down for analysis. And five, time series behaviour, which means recognising trend and seasonality in data over time.
42: First scale pair: nominal and ordinal. Both describe categories. The difference is whether the categories have a meaningful order. Nominal data is labels or names with no rank. You can only say things are the same or different. Examples are blood type, gender, product colour and country of residence. The allowed statistics are the mode and frequency counts. Ordinal data has categories with a meaningful order, but the gap between ranks is not measured or equal. Examples are customer satisfaction as low, medium or high, education level, movie star ratings, and finishing position in a race. Here you can also use the median and ranking.
43: Second pair: interval and ratio. Both are numeric with equal gaps between values. The difference is whether zero means none. Interval data has equal spacing, but zero is just a point on the scale and not nothing. Examples are temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit, the calendar year, I Q score and pH. You cannot make ratio claims, so you cannot say it is twice as hot. Ratio data has equal spacing and a true zero meaning none, so ratios and multiples are meaningful. Examples are height, weight, income, price, age and distance travelled. All statistics are allowed, including ratios.
44: Quick recap of the four scales. Nominal is named categories, like blood type. Ordinal is ordered categories, like a satisfaction rating. Interval has equal gaps but no true zero, like temperature in Celsius. Ratio has equal gaps and a true zero, like weight or income. As you move from nominal to ordinal to interval to ratio, precision increases, and so does the set of statistics you are allowed to use.
45: Next, the nature of numeric data: discrete versus continuous. Both are numeric, interval or ratio data. The difference is whether values are counted or measured. Discrete values are countable, usually whole numbers. You can list every possible value, and there is nothing in between. Examples are number of children, cars sold per day, number of defects and website visits. Continuous values are measured and can take any value within a range, limited only by the precision of measurement. Examples are height, weight, temperature, time to complete a task and distance travelled.
46: Now, how data is organised. Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns with a fixed schema, so every record has the same fields. Think of a table with I D, name and score. Examples are Excel or S Q L tables, C R M customer records and transaction ledgers. Semi structured data has tags or markers to separate elements, but no fixed table schema, so fields can vary from record to record. The example on the right is a J S O N record, where one record can have tags and a nested address while another does not. Examples are J S O N and X M L files, emails with headers plus free text, and No S Q L documents.
47: Raw text has no rows or columns of its own, so it is broken into layers before it can be analysed. The corpus is the full collection of text documents being studied, for example all customer reviews. A document is one unit of text within the corpus, for example a single review or email. A token is a word, number or punctuation mark produced by splitting the text apart, which is called tokenisation. The vocabulary, or set of terms, is the unique tokens used across the corpus after cleaning. Why does it matter? Text is unstructured by default. Typical preparation steps like lowercasing, removing stop words, and stemming or lemmatisation turn free text into structured features, like a term frequency table, that models can use.
48: A time series is data recorded at regular intervals. Two patterns to look for first are trend and seasonality. Trend is the long term direction the series is heading, upward, downward or flat, once short term noise is smoothed out. Look for a rising or falling moving average, the dashed line in the chart. Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at fixed, known intervals, for example every twelve months, driven by predictable factors like weather or holidays. Look for the same up and down wave repeating each cycle. In the chart of monthly sales over twenty four months, you can see the underlying trend rising, with a seasonal swing repeating on top of it.
49: Key takeaways. The measurement scale, from nominal to ratio, decides which statistics and maths operations are valid. Discrete data is counted in whole units, and continuous data is measured and can take any value in a range. Structured data fits a fixed schema, like tables, and semi structured data uses flexible tags, like J S O N and X M L. Text must be broken down from corpus to document to token to term before it can be analysed like structured data. And in time series, separate the steady long term trend from the repeating seasonal pattern before drawing conclusions.
